validator: draft 1 passed with no hard or soft problems; the faults below are the critic's
keep: The idea is named up front: one test, one curve, three different things on it (stiffness, yield, strength), tied back to the sling legs' tension from Forces in balance.

Stress and strain are each built from a reason (a thicker bar spreads the pull; every millimetre of a longer bar stretches the same) before they are named, with real numbers: 10 kN on a 20 mm bar is 31.8 N/mm², a quarter the area gives four times the stress.

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13). Each brief misconception has its own wrong pick: stress taken as a force (2, 6 kN), the formula upside down (2, 0.0067 N/mm²), per cent used as a fraction (6, 700 N/mm²), all or nothing springing back (8, 0 and 10 mm), stiffness confused with strength (10, bar B).

The brief's picture is followed: drag the stretch, let go anywhere, spring back to zero before yield, unload parallel and keep a permanent stretch after it; stiffness labelled as the slope and strength as the peak; the closing still shows the shaft surface going from stretched to squeezed every turn.
The analogy is from Dan's trade and reproduces the main result: resistance is a slope, a current rating is a limit, and one does not tell you the other.

Five footnotes, one a sentence, on the rules he would look up (proportional at low stress, the modulus, yield, the 0.2% offset, tensile strength); no source named in the words; fatigue, necking and the factor of safety are stated plainly as textbook facts.
fix: Causal step skipped: 'the bar springs back along a line parallel to the straight start' gives no reason. Say the part that springs back is still the elastic part, with the same stiffness, so it gives back only the stress ÷ Young's modulus.
Causal step skipped: 'the force falls until it breaks' after the peak. Say the neck's area shrinks faster than the metal gets stronger, so the force it can carry falls.
Causal step skipped: why a load far below yield can crack a part. Say a tiny flaw or sharp corner carries a higher stress than the rest, and the crack grows there a little each cycle.

The interactive shows the effect (a permanent stretch) more than its cause. On letting go, split the stretch into its springback and its permanent part, each labelled in mm, so he sees the springy part is the small elastic share.
Talks about instead of teaching: 'plots the whole story as one curve' is vague. Say what the test records: the force and the stretch, all the way to the break.

The analogy's breaks sentence 'running it over heats it rather than changing it for good straight away' is clumsy and half true. Say a rating is set by heat and how the cable is installed, while a bar past yield keeps a permanent stretch that no volts-against-amps line shows.

faults.causalStepSkipped: three places: the parallel unloading line, the falling force after the peak, fatigue below yield
faults.falseAbsolutes: none found: 'any pull stretches a bar a little' and 'springs back to its first length' are true where used; 'never load past its safe working load' is a safety rule
faults.interactiveShowsOnlyEffect: partly: split the stretch on letting go into springback and permanent stretch
faults.thinResearch: none: footnotes sit on words their quotes support; steel's modulus, necking, the factor of safety and fatigue are unfootnoted textbook facts stated plainly
faults.talksAboutInsteadOfTeaching: one: 'plots the whole story as one curve'

shape.misconceptionShownFailing: yes in the puzzles; explain says stress is not a force and a metal can be stiff and weak
